title.en: The Magician Who Bought the Birds' Voices

region.en: Yoruba forest grove (symbolic pin: grove near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴林間樹叢（象徵定位：伊費近郊樹叢）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XV

summary.en: A jealous magician envies the songs of a grove's brown birds and tricks them into trading their voices — stored in a calabash he swallows — for brightly coloured feathers. His singing draws hearers from far and near, while the most beautiful birds remain quite unable to sing.
summary.zh: 巫師嫉妒林間褐鳥的歌聲，以「換得彩羽」為餌，誘使群鳥將聲音裝入葫蘆交出，他一口吞下，從此歌喉甜美，聽者雲集；而最豔麗的鳥兒卻自此啞然無聲。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A magician once passed through a grove where a great many brown birds filled the air with songs. He sat and listened, enraptured, but in the end became very jealous, for he himself could not sing. He felt he must by some means possess the voices of the singing birds, so he called them together and said it grieved him that the gods had given them such poor, ugly brown feathers — how happy they would be if they were brilliantly coloured with red, blue, orange, and green! The birds agreed that it was a great pity to be so ugly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XV (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: The magician suggested that by his charms he could give them beautiful feathers in exchange for their voices, which were of little use since nobody came into the grove to hear them. The birds desired the beauty he promised and foolishly agreed; their voices were placed in a large calabash, and their dull brown feathers were turned to orange, green, and red. The magician hurried away and swallowed the calabash's contents, and from that day he had an exceedingly sweet voice, so that people came from far and near to listen. But the birds were satisfied with their bright feathers — and this is why the most beautiful birds are quite unable to sing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XV (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba royal court (symbolic pin: Oyo palace)
region.zh: 約魯巴王廷（象徵定位：奧約王宮）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XVI

summary.en: When a war-king refuses to let his three magician retainers go home, two vanish by magic; the third, Elenre, cannot be harmed — sword breaks, arm withers, spear crumples, rock rolls away. Betrayed by his wife's hint (a blade of thatch will cut him), he is beheaded, but his head sticks to the king's hand and devours his food until a wiser magician greets it respectfully. The head falls, becomes Elenre's river, and the treacherous wife is changed into a stagnant pool.
summary.zh: 戰時為王造符的三位巫師戰後請歸，王不許。兩位各顯神通遁走；第三位埃倫雷刀不能傷、矛不能刺、石不能壓。其妻洩密——以茅草一片即可斷其首——巫師人頭落地，卻黏在王手上，吞盡王的飲食，群巫無策。唯有一位謙卑的巫師致敬於頭顱，頭顱方落，化為「埃倫雷河」；背妻則化為不流的死水潭。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; magic-contest tale with a place-name etiology (Odo Elenre). Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A certain King had engaged in a series of wars, during which he employed three magicians to make charms for him. At the war's end they humbly asked to be allowed to return home; the King foolishly refused, and the magicians replied: "We asked your permission out of courtesy, O King, but we can very easily depart without it." The first fell on the ground and disappeared; the second threw a ball of twine into the air, climbed up the thread, and vanished likewise. The third, Elenre, remained standing. "It is your turn to disappear," said the King, trembling with anger, "or I will slay you." "You cannot harm me," replied the magician.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVI (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ordered beheaded, Elenre saw the sword break in two and the executioner's arm wither; the spear crumpled; the great rock rolled over his body like a child's ball. At last his wife confessed his secret: a blade of thatch grass could cut off his head. This was done — but the head stuck fast to the King's hand and consumed all his food and drink, so that the King seemed likely to die. Magicians summoned from all over the kingdom were laughed at by the head, until one prostrated himself: "Who am I to oppose you, great Elenre? I come only because the King commands me." "You are wiser than all the rest!" said Elenre, and the head fell to the ground and became a flowing river called to this day Odo Elenre, Elenre's river. His treacherous wife was likewise changed into a river, but Elenre commanded it not to flow, and it became a stagnant pool.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVI (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba royal town (symbolic pin: palace near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴王城（象徵定位：奧約附近王宮）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XVII

summary.en: Barren queen Isokun wanders to every shrine of tree, stream and rock seeking a child, and is refused. Stealing a two-day-old baby by the wayside, she passes it off as the king's heir amid palace rejoicing — until the hungry baby's cries draw its true mother, who snatches it to her breast; the fraud is exposed and Isokun flees the palace for ever.
summary.zh: 無子的王妃伊索昆遍訪草木溪石之神的聖所求子，皆遭拒絕。歸途中她偷走路邊一名出生兩日的嬰兒，謊稱為王誕下麟兒，宮中慶宴大作。嬰兒啼飢，生母循聲而至，一把攬兒入懷即時止啼。真相大白，伊索昆羞愧出逃，永不回宮。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; shrine-circuit and stolen-child tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A certain King Dekun had a wife named Isokun who bore him no children, on which account there was great unhappiness in the palace. One day Isokun disappeared and was absent for many weeks: she had set out to visit the shrines of all the gods, in the hope that one of them would promise her a child. But though she travelled far and wide, the gods of all the trees and streams and rocks refused her prayer. Nearing home, she came upon a poor woman asleep by the wayside with her baby two days old. Isokun stole the baby and hastened to the palace, where she informed the King that she had disappeared in order to give him the joyous surprise of his little son. There were great rejoicings; sacrifices were made and the drums beat loudly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Meanwhile the real mother awoke and found her baby gone; she searched every house and at last insisted on entering the palace, where all were celebrating the arrival of the King's heir. All this time the baby cried with hunger, and Isokun, unable to feed him, invented other reasons for the crying. Drawn by the cries, the mother entered and snatched the baby to her breast, where it was at once contented. In a few moments the deception was made clear; the mother departed with her child, and Isokun, ashamed and fearing the King's anger, fled from the palace and never returned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: The Twin Brothers of King Ajaka

region.en: Yoruba river town (symbolic pin: riverside near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴河城（象徵定位：奧約附近河畔）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XVIII

summary.en: Under the cruel custom that twins must be destroyed, King Ajaka secretly exiles his favourite wife and her twin sons. When the father dies heirless, the brothers cast stones for the throne; the winner reigns, sends for his twin — then, jealous, drowns him. A fish rises singing "Your brother lies here," and when the king kills it, the river itself sings the same words before the court, and the murderer takes poison in disgrace.
summary.zh: 按當時孿生子女須被處死的殘俗，阿賈卡王暗中將愛妃與雙生二子送至僻地。父王駕崩無嗣，兄弟以擲石決定王位；登基者迎回胞弟，卻因嫉妒將他推入河中溺斃。魚兒浮水唱「你兄弟在此」，王殺魚；河水又當廷高唱同一句歌。真相大白，惡弟遭民唾棄，服毒而亡。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition. Twins (Ibeji) hold a special honoured place in Yoruba religion; this tale is set in the old era when the twin-taboo operated, and echoes the twins motif cluster. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A certain Yoruba King, Ajaka, had a favourite wife; but she gave birth to twins. At that time it was the universal custom to destroy twins immediately at birth, and the mother with them. But the King had not the heart to put this cruel law into execution, and secretly charged one of his nobles to conduct the royal mother and her babes to a remote place where they might live in safety. There the twin brothers grew to manhood, loving one another greatly; when one began to speak, the other completed his phrase, so harmonious were their thoughts. Their mother, before she died, told them of their royal birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVIII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: When news came that their father was dead leaving no heir, they decided to cast stones for the throne. The lot fell on the younger, who became King and sent for his brother to share his splendour. But jealousy overcame brotherly affection: walking by the river, he pushed his brother into the water, where he was drowned, and gave out that he had left the country in his favour. Some time later, passing the spot, he saw a fish rise and sing: "Your brother lies here." He killed it with a sharp stone. But another day, attended by his nobles under the royal umbrella, the river itself rose into waves and sang the same words; the courtiers looked into the water and found the body of the King. The secret disclosed, the wicked brother was rejected in horror by his people, and at this disgrace took poison and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XVIII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Leopard Got His Spots

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: undergrowth near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊密林）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XIX

summary.en: Pursued by the hunter Akiti, the lion-coloured leopard eats the roots of a magic plant and becomes invulnerable — but at every poisoned arrow that strikes him a dark mark appears, until his body carries so many arrow-marks that among the trees he looks like the mingling of sun and shadow.
summary.zh: 被獵人阿基提追捕的豹原與獅同色、身無斑紋；牠服食仙草之根變得刀槍不入，但每中一箭便留一道黑痕。箭痕累積滿身，豹穿行林間時恰似日光與樹影交錯——豹紋由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: At one time the Leopard was coloured like a lion, and he had no dark markings; but he was pursued by Akiti, the renowned hunter, and feared that he might be slain. To avoid this he ate the roots of a certain magic plant, which had the effect of making him invulnerable to any of the hunter's weapons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIX (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon afterwards Akiti saw him slipping through the dense undergrowth, and though he shot his poisoned arrows, the Leopard escaped — but where each arrow struck him, there appeared a dark mark. Now, though hunters still pursue him, he is rarely caught, and his body is covered with the marks of the arrows, so that as he goes among the trees he looks exactly like the mingling of the sun and shadow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XIX (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Another Story of the Leopard's Spots

region.en: Yoruba village compound (symbolic pin: bathing-hut near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落院落（象徵定位：伊費近郊浴棚）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XX

summary.en: A dark-skinned leopard prowls round a hut where a woman is bathing; she flings her soap-filled loofah at him. He flees — but to this day the leopard is flecked with soap from foot to head.
summary.zh: 一頭黑豹繞著婦人沐浴的小屋打轉，欲撲食屋中人；婦人驚呼間將滿是皂沫的絲瓜絡擲去。豹負皂而逃——至今豹身自足至首仍斑斑點點，盡是皂漬。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; humorous animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: According to another story, Leopard once had a very dark skin. He was prowling one day in a beautiful compound when he noticed a little hut in which a lady was taking her bath. Round and round the hut Leopard walked, waiting for an opportunity to spring in and seize his victim, for he was hungry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XX (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: But as he passed the opening of the hut, the lady saw him and, uttering a scream of terror, threw at him her loofah, which was full of soap. She flung it at him and he fled — but to this day the Leopard still is flecked with soap from foot to head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XX (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: The Head That Borrowed a Body

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: roads between village and river, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費與河岸之間的村路）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXI

summary.en: In a land of bodiless jumping Heads, one Head sets out to see the world, politely borrowing a slave's body, a sleeper's arms, and a fisherman's legs. Whole again, he wins a bride at the dancing-ground — then returns each borrowed part on the journey home, and his horrified wife runs away, leaving the Head alone for ever.
summary.zh: 在某國度，人人只有會跳躍的頭而無身軀。一顆頭偷偷出遊，依次向老婦借得奴隸的身體、向樹下沉睡的青年借得雙臂、向漁夫借得雙腿，拼成完人，在舞場贏得美眷。歸途中他一一奉還所借：腿還漁夫，臂還青年，身還老婦。新娘見丈夫只剩一顆頭，驚恐逃去，頭顱再也追不上，永失所愛。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; wonder tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There is a certain country where the inhabitants have heads but no bodies. The Heads move about by jumping along the ground, but they never go very far. One of the Heads desired to see the world, so he set out one morning secretly. He saw an old woman looking out of the door of a hut and asked her to lend him a body; she willingly lent him the body of her slave. Later he came upon a young man sleeping under a tree and asked to borrow a pair of arms, as he did not appear to be using them; the young man agreed. At the river-bank where fishermen sat mending their net, one of them lent him a pair of legs. Now he had legs, arms, and a body, and appeared like any other man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXI (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the evening he reached a town and saw maidens dancing while onlookers threw coins to those they favoured. The Head threw all his coins to one dancer, who so admired his handsome form that she consented to marry him and live in his own country. Next day they set out, but at the river-bank the stranger took off his legs and gave them back to the fisherman; later he returned his arms to the young man sleeping under the tree; finally he gave up his body at the old woman's cottage. When the bride saw that her husband was merely a Head, she was filled with horror and ran away as fast as she could go — and now that he had neither body, arms, nor legs, the Head could not overtake her, and so lost her for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXI (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊院落）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXII

summary.en: Lazy, nosy Ole lets the ants build a pillar in his compound so he can perch on top and spy on his neighbours without moving. While he sits there crowing, the ants demolish his house and everything in it; he becomes the village laughing-stock — "Ku ijoko!" greetings on your sitting! — and dies of it.
summary.zh: 懶惰又多事的奧雷任由螞蟻在院中築起高柱，只為坐上柱頂窺探鄰居動靜。他終日高坐唱道「我如大酋長，萬事盡入眼」，螻蟻卻趁機啃光他的房屋糧食。村人見他皆喊「庫伊佐科——恭賀高坐！」，不久他便羞愧（或懶）而死。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; moral folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There was a certain lazy and disagreeable man whom everyone called Ole, the Lazy one. He liked to profit by the work of others and was very inquisitive about other people's affairs. Once he saw that the ants had begun building a pillar in the compound of his house; though they destroyed all the plants and stripped the trees, Ole would not trouble to kill them or break down their pillar. Instead he thought: "When the ants have made this pillar very high, I will sit on the top of it, and then I shall be able to see all that my neighbours are doing without leaving my compound."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: This thought pleased him, and each day the pillar grew higher until the ants ceased building and began again elsewhere. Ole climbed up and spent the whole day observing his neighbours, singing: "Here sit I like a great Chief, and I see all things!" But while he sat on the pillar, the ants began to demolish his house and all that it contained, and soon nothing was left of his food and possessions. Ole thus became the laughing-stock of the village, and everyone who saw him cried: "Ku ijoko!" — Greetings to you on your sitting! Soon afterwards he died, and it is not known to this day whether he died of shame or of laziness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Hunter Who Became a Boa-Constrictor

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: hunting paths near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊獵徑）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXIII

summary.en: Too old to hunt, Ogunfunminire buys a pair of magic pots from a magician: dipping his head in the first turns him into a boa-constrictor to hunt the forest, the second restores him at nightfall. His family discovers the secret and, horrified, overturns both pots — and the serpent glide that was once their father disappears into the forest for ever.
summary.zh: 老獵人奧貢芬米尼雷不願捨棄狩獵之樂，向巫師求得兩只魔罐：晨將頭探入第一罐即化為蟒入林捕獵，夜以第二罐復形。家人窺破後驚駭不已，其子一怒踢翻雙罐。化蟒的他無法還原，繞宅數日尋覓咒液不果，終於沒入林中，家人再無所見。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; shapeshifting tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Ogunfunminire, the famous hunter, lived to such a great age that he was no longer able to go into the forest and chase the deer and the leopard. Life had no other pleasure for him than hunting, so he went to a magician and asked for a charm which would enable him to continue his occupation. The magician gave him two pots, each containing a charm: every day Ogunfunminire dipped his head into the first pot and was at once transformed into a boa-constrictor, in which form he glided into the forest and hunted to his heart's content; at night he dipped his head into the second pot and became a man again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: This went on for a long time unknown to the old hunter's family; but when at last they chanced to discover the secret, they were filled with horror, and his son in a rage kicked at the pots and overturned them both. Ogunfunminire was hunting in the forest at that moment; returning, he found the magic pots empty and was filled with dismay, for he had no means of regaining his human form. For some days the boa-constrictor glided about near the house, seeking a few drops of the charm, but in vain, and at last he disappeared into the forest and was never seen by his family again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Oluronbi's Broken Vow to the Iroko

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the iroko grove outside the village)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（象徵定位：村外伊羅科樹叢）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXIV

summary.en: A childless village begs the Iroko-man for children, promising gifts; young Oluronbi promises her first child. Children come — but she and her husband cannot give up their beautiful daughter. Passing through the forest, she is seized and changed into a small brown bird singing of the broken promise, until her wood-carver husband carves a lifelike doll with a gold chain that the Iroko-man accepts in exchange.
summary.zh: 多年無孩的村莊齊赴伊羅科樹前求子，許諾獻上穀物山羊；木雕匠之妻奧魯倫比卻許諾「頭胎孩子」。孩子們降生了，夫妻卻捨不得交出最美的女兒。奧魯倫比路過樹叢，被樹靈捉住化為小褐鳥，終日唱著毀諾之歌。丈夫深思多日，雕出逼真木偶、繫上金鏈置於樹下；樹靈信以為真，將鳥還為人形，攜「孩兒」入林，奧魯倫比得以還家，自此再不敢入林。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; vow-to-spirit tale bound to iroko veneration. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: In a certain village no children had been born for many years, and the people were greatly distressed. At last all the women went together into the forest, to the magic tree, the Iroko, and implored the spirit of the tree to help them. The Iroko-man asked what gifts they would bring if he consented, and the women eagerly promised corn, yams, fruit, goats, and sheep; but Oluronbi, the young wife of a wood-carver, promised to bring her first child. In due course children came to the village, and the most beautiful of all was the one born to Oluronbi. She and her husband so greatly loved their child that they could not consent to give it up to the Iroko-man; the other women took their promised gifts, but Oluronbi took nothing to propitiate the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIV (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Alas! one day as Oluronbi passed through the forest, the Iroko-man seized her and changed her into a small brown bird, which sat on the branches of the tree and plaintively sang: "One promised a sheep, one promised a goat, one promised fruit — but Oluronbi promised her child." When the wood-carver heard the song he realized what had happened. After thinking for many days he carved a large wooden doll, like a real child, with a small gold chain round its neck, covered it with a beautiful native cloth, and laid it at the foot of the tree. The Iroko-man thought this was Oluronbi's child, transformed the little bird once more into a woman, and snatched the doll up into the branches. Oluronbi joyfully returned home, and was careful never to stray into the forest again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIV (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (symbolic pin: site of the obelisk outside Oyo)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（象徵定位：奧約城外的石柱遺址）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXV

summary.en: Oranyan, founder of Oyo, leaves his son in charge during a long expedition; believed dead, he returns to hear the Kakaki trumpet sounded for a new king — his own son. Preferring his son's happiness to his throne, he withdraws to obscure retirement, and only at his death is the truth known. The grieving young king raises the obelisk still called the Staff of Oranyan.
summary.zh: 奧約城的建立者奧蘭揚王遠征未歸，國人以為他已戰死，立其子為王。他歷盡艱辛返抵城外，卻聽見只為國王而鳴的卡卡基號角。田間農人答道：「奧蘭揚之子已為王，其父早歿於戰陣。」他甘願讓位，攜少數隨從退居僻野，至死方為其子所知。年輕的國王悲痛父親的犧牲，於其身故之地立碑，即今猶存的「奧蘭揚之柱」。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Staff of Oranyan (Opa Oranyan) is a real monolith at Oyo-Ile associated with the Alaafin line. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Oranyan, a brave and warlike King, founded the city of Oyo. As it was necessary for him to lead an expedition to a distant part of his kingdom, he left his son in charge of the capital during his absence. But the King was away for so long a period that it was thought he and his soldiers must have perished, and at last the people made his son King, who for some time ruled them wisely and happily. However, Oranyan was not dead, and after many delays and hardships he again drew near to Oyo with his few surviving followers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXV (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: As he approached the city he was startled to hear the notes of the Kakaki trumpet, which is sounded for the King alone. A man working in the fields told him: "Do you not know that the son of Oranyan is King, and rules over us wisely and well? His father was killed in battle many months ago." Desiring his son's happiness more than his own, the old King retraced his steps and settled down with his few friends in humble retirement in a remote part of the country; only at Oranyan's death was his presence made known to his son. The young King, grieving at his noble father's sacrifice, erected an obelisk over the spot where he died, and the monument, known as the Staff of Oranyan, is still to be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXV (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Elephant Got His Trunk

region.en: Yoruba forest (symbolic pin: watering place near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴森林（象徵定位：伊費近郊獸徑）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXVI

summary.en: Inquisitive Elephant pokes his short snout into a dark hole and is seized by the great snake within; his wife and he himself pull so hard against the serpent that his nose is drawn out into the long trunk all elephants carry now. The monkey who tried to imitate him was simply swallowed.
summary.zh: 好奇的大象把短吻探入地洞，被洞中巨蛇咬住不放。象妻拉尾、大象前掙，一拉一扯之間，象鼻被拉長成今日的長鼻。起初大象羞於見同伴，如今眾獸反而豔羨。愛模仿的猴子也去探洞，卻被巨蛇一口吞下，從此再無獸敢學象。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; animal etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Now it is a matter of common knowledge that Elephant has a long trunk, which he uses both as a nose and as a sort of hand. But he was once without it, and had a very ordinary short snout like other animals. Elephant was always inquisitive and went sniffing about the forest, prying into the secrets of the other animals. One day he came across a dark hole in the ground, and into this hole he poked his nose, to see what was there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVI (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: He at once regretted his curiosity, for a large snake who lived in the hole seized him by the nose and tried to swallow him. Elephant made a great uproar, and his wife came rushing to his assistance; she seized his tail and pulled and pulled, and Elephant himself pulled and pulled, but the snake would not leave go. And as a result, Elephant's nose was drawn out into the long trunk which he still has. At first he was ashamed to appear in the forest, but now the other animals envy him. One day the monkey, which imitates everybody, looked down the same hole thinking a long trunk would let him swing from the trees by his nose — but the big snake swallowed him, and since then nobody else has tried to imitate Elephant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVI (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba river country (symbolic pin: staked weir near a Yoruba river)
region.zh: 約魯巴河鄉（象徵定位：河中魚籠堤堰）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXVII

summary.en: An unlucky fisherman shares his supper with a silent stranger who vanishes; from that evening his baskets overflow with fish, until the last basket holds a monstrous fish that speaks: it is the King of the fishes, the stranger he had befriended, come to reward his kindness.
summary.zh: 運蹇的漁夫在河中下籠，日日空手。某日他遇一沉默的外鄉人臥於岸邊，非但未傷害他，還分與晚餐；外鄉人不語而食，倏忽隱去。當晚起魚籠滿溢，第三日末籠中竟有一尾會說話的巨魚：「你忘了那受你款待的旅人嗎？我正是魚王，特來報答你的善意。」言畢躍入河中，漁夫自此富足。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; gratitude-of-animals tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Across a certain river a poor fisherman set a row of stakes, and on each stake was fastened a basket in which he hoped to trap the fishes as they swam down the river. But his luck was very bad, and every evening he went from basket to basket in his canoe to find no fishes, or only a few very small ones. This made him very sad, and he was forced to live frugally. One day he found a stranger lying asleep on the river-bank; instead of killing the stranger, the fisherman spoke kindly to him and invited him to share his evening meal. The stranger ate and drank but spoke no word at all, and quite suddenly vanished — only the remains of the meal convinced the fisherman he had not been dreaming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next evening the baskets were overflowing with fish, and the same thing occurred day after day. On the third day the last basket contained a single monstrous fish. "Do you not know me?" said the fish. "Have you forgotten the stranger whom you treated so courteously? It was I, and I am the King of the fishes. I am grateful for your kindness and intend to reward you." Then the fish jumped into the river with a great splash; but ever afterwards the fishing-baskets were full every evening, and the fisherman became rich and prosperous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ten Goldsmiths and the Ear of Golden Corn

region.en: Yoruba craft village (symbolic pin: smithing quarter near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴工匠村（象徵定位：伊費近郊金匠坊）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXVIII

summary.en: A dying goldsmith sets his ten sons a contest: the most skilful shall keep the village trade. Nine present chains, knives, caskets and rings; the eldest, Ayo, seems to have made nothing — until the last hour, when the family sits round the fire parching corn and the father's full pipe of corn proves to be pure gold. Ayo keeps the bench.
summary.zh: 垂死的金匠命十子競技，技藝最高者可承父業。九人獻上金鏈、小刀、寶匣、蛇形戒環；長子阿約卻兩手空空，遭父嚴斥。阿約請全家最後一次圍火烘玉米講故事——父親拿起身邊滿滿一管玉米，竟發現是純金所鑄。技藝瞞過眾人，阿約當之無愧繼承父業。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; craft-competition tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A goldsmith in a small village had ten sons, to all of whom he taught his trade. When the old man was dying he called the ten around him: in this small village there was not enough work for ten goldsmiths, so the most skilful should remain in his place while the rest went out into the world. He allowed them a month to make some article of gold, and at the end of that time would judge which had been most skilfully executed. When the articles were laid before him, he found there were only nine: the eldest son, Ayo, had produced nothing. After bitterly reproaching him, the father prepared to judge the work of the other brothers; but Ayo stepped forward and begged him to wait another hour. "Meanwhile, Father, let us sit round the fire all together for the last time, parching corn and telling stories."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVIII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: As they seated themselves on the ground, the father took up a full pipe of corn which lay near him. What was his astonishment when he tried to pick the grains to discover that it was made of gold! For this was what Ayo had made, and he had prepared the little trick to test the perfection of his work: so skilfully was it executed that all had been deceived, thinking it a real ear of corn. On this account the father and the nine brothers all agreed that Ayo's work was certainly the best. Thus Ayo took his father's place, and the rest set out in different directions to seek their fortune.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXVIII (1929); not verbatim.
